newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU conference to combat expanding trade in women.
newsitem.headline: EU conference to combat expanding trade in women.

text.p: Trafficking in women for sex in the European Union is becoming recognised as as a problem as serious as drugs or arms smuggling, the head of an EU panel said on Thursday.
"This is luckily slowly but surely being realised," Nel van Dijk, chairwoman of the European Parliament's Woman's Rights Committee told Dutch radio.
"But it is naturally also true that...there has not been much policy developed yet in this area."
Van Dik spoke as delegates gathered in the Hague for an international conference to promote a coordinated crackdown on trafficking in women.

After two days of closed-door discussions between interest groups, police and observers from prospective EU member states in eastern Europe, the conference will on Saturday bring in EU ministers to try to hammer out a code of conduct for member states.

Figures from the International Organization for Migration show some 500,000 women were trafficked to the EU for sexual exploitation in 1995 and the European Commission recognises that the trend is on the rise.

"Thousands of women are being trafficked from developing countries and Central and Eastern Europe to Western Europe and brought into quasi-slavery," the Commission said in a recent report to the European Parliament.

"Trafficking in women for sexual exploitation is an increasing type of international organised crime generating high profits with relatively low forms of risk. Only a minority of cases are reported and convictions of traffickers are rare."

Particular concerns for the EU are the increase in the numbers of women being trafficked from eastern Europe and the emergence of established, well-connected and often violent criminal gangs running the trade.

"There are large enterprises and international networks creating a sophisticated and well-organised 'industry', with political support and economic resources in countries of origin, transit and destination," the Commission said.
Proposals for an EU code of conduct will be presented by the Dutch government, which has made the issue a priority of its six-month EU presidency.
A key thrust of the Dutch approach is to target traffickers, rather than victims, by ensuring exploited women living illegally in the EU can seek help without risking immediate deportation.

"The current policies in the majority of member states deter women from reporting to the authorities, as they are faced with arrest, detention and expulsion as illegal aliens and/or prostitutes," a background document says.
"Too often it is the victim who turns out to stand trial instead of the offender."

The Netherlands, which tolerates but closely monitors prostitution, grants temporary residence permits to women forced into the sex trade to allow them to testify against their captors. Belgium takes a similar view.
"If you simply send these women home, then you can be just about certain that the very same woman-trafficking syndicate will make sure that the vacancy you create will be filled," Van Dijk said.
